hook.line: Tomás has just opened the first of Rosa's letters, and every sentence in it looks backward: what she had said, what had already happened before she wrote. To tell a story that reaches back before its own beginning, you need one more past.
hook.es: No sabía que Rosa había escrito tantas cartas.
hook.en: I didn't know Rosa had written so many letters.

examples.es: Cuando llegué, Vale ya se había ido.
examples.en: When I arrived, Vale had already left.
I had never seen so many people.
Had you already spoken with Hernando?

rule:
English says *had* plus a verb: *had left*, *had seen*. Spanish does the same with two parts.

*había*, *habías*, *había*, *habíamos*, *habían* + the ending you already know from *he estado*:
*-ar* verbs: *-ado* (*hablado*)
*-er* and *-ir* verbs: *-ido* (*comido*, *salido*)

The odd ones are the same as before: *escrito*, *visto*, *hecho*, *dicho*, *vuelto*.

Use it for something that was already finished before another moment in the past: *Cuando llegué* is the moment, *ya se había ido* is what came earlier.

Nothing goes between the two parts, and little words go in front: *ya se había ido*, *nunca había visto*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the pluperfect, or past perfect: the past of the past. It is the *he estado* form moved back one step in time.

options: Rosa has already read the letter.

options: When we arrived, the café was opening.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Cuando llegué, Vale ya se ___ ido.* (*había* or *habían*) When I arrived, Vale had already left.
yourTurn.answer: Cuando llegué, Vale ya se había ido.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Nunca ___ visto tanta gente.* (*había* or *habíamos*) I had never seen so many people.
yourTurn.why: The speaker is *I*, so *había*; *habíamos* would mean *we*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say to a friend: Had you already spoken with Hernando?
Say: Rosa had never traveled alone.
accept: Rosa no había viajado nunca sola.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative, with *todavía*: *Vale ya había llegado.*
yourTurn.why: *No* goes straight before *había*; the two parts stay together.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about *they* (*ellos*): *Vale ya se había ido.*
yourTurn.why: More than one person means *habían*, and *se* stays in front.

pitfalls.wrong: Cuando llegué, Vale ya se fue.
pitfalls.right: Cuando llegué, Vale ya se había ido.
pitfalls.why: Almost. If it was already finished before the other moment, Spanish wants *había* plus the ending.
*Escribir* has an odd ending, *escrito*, the same one you use after *he*.
Little words like *se* go in front of *había*, not between the two parts.
*Nunca* goes before *había*; nothing can sit between *had* and the verb ending.

personal: Think of this morning. Write two things you had already done before you left home, starting with *Ya había…*, and one thing you hadn't done yet, with *Todavía no había…*.
